questions.prompt: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to track nodes awaiting visit?

options.text: A first-in, first-out queue.
options.explanation: Breadth-first search processes nodes in the exact order they are discovered using a FIFO queue.

options.text: A last-in, first-out call stack.
options.explanation: A stack is used by depth-first search, not breadth-first search.

options.text: A key-value hash map table.
options.explanation: A hash map stores key-value associations rather than a sequence of frontier nodes.

options.text: A binary maximum heap tree.
options.explanation: A max heap prioritizes extreme values rather than level-by-level traversal order.

questions.prompt: What is the visit order of an in-order depth-first search traversal on a binary tree?

options.text: Root node, then left child, then right child.
options.explanation: Visiting root first is pre-order traversal.

options.text: Left child, then root node, then right child.
options.explanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree first, then the current node, then the right subtree.

options.text: Left child, then right child, then root node.
options.explanation: Visiting children before the root is post-order traversal.

options.text: Root node, then right child, then left child.
options.explanation: Visiting right before left is a reverse pre-order traversal.

questions.prompt: Why does an in-order traversal on a valid binary search tree visit nodes in sorted order?

options.text: Because the queue automatically sorts all incoming integers.
options.explanation: In-order depth-first search uses a stack, not a sorting queue.

options.text: Because every parent node holds a smaller value than both children.
options.explanation: In a binary search tree, only the left child is smaller than the parent.

options.text: Because all smaller left values are visited before the root and right.
options.explanation: A binary search tree enforces that left values are smaller and right values are larger, matching in-order sequence.

options.text: Because post-order steps swap inverted values back into order.
options.explanation: Post-order traversal is a different walk and does not reorder nodes.

questions.prompt: Which traversal is best suited for finding the shortest path in an unweighted tree?

options.text: Pre-order depth-first search.
options.explanation: Pre-order DFS may traverse deeply down an unpromising branch first.

options.text: Post-order depth-first search.
options.explanation: Post-order DFS visits bottom leaves first without considering branch distance.

options.text: In-order depth-first search.
options.explanation: In-order DFS follows subtree structure instead of shortest path distance.

options.text: Breadth-first search.
options.explanation: Breadth-first search visits nodes level by level, ensuring the first target reached has the shortest path.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum call stack memory used by recursive DFS on a balanced tree of N nodes?

options.text: O(log N) space, matching the tree height.
options.explanation: A balanced binary tree with N nodes has height log N, so the call stack holds at most log N frames.

options.text: O(N) space, matching the leaf node count.
options.explanation: O(N) space occurs on a skewed tree, not a balanced tree.

options.text: O(1) space, because recursion uses heap memory.
options.explanation: Recursive function calls consume system call stack memory proportional to tree depth.

options.text: O(N squared) space, because each level doubles.
options.explanation: Call stack frames correspond to path depth, not squared node count.

questions.prompt: In Swift, what performance problem occurs when calling queue.removeFirst() on an Array in BFS?

options.text: It throws an unhandled fatal runtime error.
options.explanation: Calling removeFirst on a non-empty array does not throw a runtime error.

options.text: It shifts all remaining elements, taking O(K) time per pop.
options.explanation: Swift arrays have contiguous storage, so removing the first element takes linear time proportional to count.

options.text: It creates a strong memory retain cycle between nodes.
options.explanation: Array element removal does not establish retain cycles between tree nodes.

options.text: It reverses the child pointer references on the tree.
options.explanation: Popping an array element does not alter pointers inside TreeNode instances.

questions.prompt: How can you isolate nodes into discrete tiers during a breadth-first search?

options.text: By inserting nil separators after every odd-numbered node.
options.explanation: Arbitrary nil insertions clutter queue logic and break boundary conditions.

options.text: By sorting the queue after each child node is inserted.
options.explanation: Sorting the queue introduces unnecessary O(K log K) overhead and disrupts FIFO order.

options.text: By capturing queue.count before running the inner loop for that level.
options.explanation: Snapshoting queue.count gives the exact count of nodes belonging to the current level before new children are enqueued.

options.text: By clearing the queue completely before visiting child nodes.
options.explanation: Clearing the queue loses references to unvisited branches.

questions.prompt: Which traversal order is most natural for calculating the height of each subtree bottom-up?

options.text: Breadth-first search from the root.
options.explanation: BFS works top-down level by level, making bottom-up height aggregation awkward.

options.text: Pre-order traversal from the root.
options.explanation: Pre-order visits the parent before knowing the height of either child.

options.text: In-order traversal from the root.
options.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the root before the right subtree has been calculated.

options.text: Post-order traversal from the root.
options.explanation: Post-order evaluates left and right subtrees before their parent, enabling clean bottom-up calculation.

questions.prompt: Why are Swift tree nodes usually modeled with a final class rather than a struct?

options.text: Classes allow recursive reference pointers without indirect enum wrappers.
options.explanation: Structs cannot directly hold recursive stored properties of their own type without infinite size.

options.text: Structs cannot be stored inside Swift collections or arrays.
options.explanation: Swift structs work seamlessly with arrays and sets.

options.text: Classes execute on background threads by default in Swift.
options.explanation: Classes do not change dispatch thread behavior automatically.

options.text: Structs do not support optional properties like left and right.
options.explanation: Structs fully support optional properties.

questions.prompt: What risk arises when traversing a completely skewed tree using recursive DFS?

options.text: The tree values automatically flip their sign.
options.explanation: Tree traversal does not modify node values.

options.text: The call stack grows to O(N), risking stack overflow.
options.explanation: A skewed tree acts like a linked list with depth N, causing deep recursive frames.

options.text: The queue consumes O(N squared) heap space.
options.explanation: DFS uses a stack rather than a breadth queue.

options.text: The Swift compiler rejects the recursive function.
options.explanation: Recursive tree traversal functions compile without issue.

questions.prompt: When comparing peak memory consumption on a very wide binary tree, which traversal is leaner?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: Breadth-first search, because queues use contiguous buffers.
options.explanation: On a wide tree, BFS holds the entire widest level in memory, which can approach N/2 nodes.

options.text: Level-order search, because parents are discarded immediately.
options.explanation: Level-order search is BFS and must hold all nodes of the next level.

options.text: Depth-first search, because its memory is bounded by tree height.
options.explanation: DFS only stores the path from root to current leaf, which is O(H) and much smaller than tree width on wide trees.

options.text: Both traversals use identical memory regardless of shape.
options.explanation: Tree topology significantly shifts the memory balance between BFS (width) and DFS (height).

questions.prompt: How can you validate whether a binary tree is a valid Binary Search Tree (BST)?

options.text: Check if node.left.val is smaller than node.val at every node.
options.explanation: Checking only immediate children fails when a distant descendant violates the ancestor boundary.

options.text: Count the total number of left nodes and right nodes.
options.explanation: Node counts do not reflect whether values satisfy ordering invariants.

options.text: Perform breadth-first search and check if each level is sorted.
options.explanation: BFS levels are not sorted in a BST because values cross different subtrees.

options.text: Pass allowable min and max range bounds down during DFS traversal.
options.explanation: Every node must fall strictly between valid minimum and maximum boundaries passed down from ancestors.

questions.prompt: What is the primary motivation for writing an iterative DFS traversal with an explicit Array stack?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: To prevent call stack overflow crashes on deeply nested trees.
options.explanation: An explicit array stack allocates heap memory, which is much larger than the restricted thread call stack.

options.text: To convert the algorithm time complexity from O(N) to O(1).
options.explanation: Visiting N nodes always requires O(N) time.

options.text: To satisfy Swift 6 Sendable protocol thread restrictions.
options.explanation: Iterative stacks do not automatically make node classes Sendable.

options.text: To visit nodes in breadth-first sequence rather than depth-first.
options.explanation: A stack still yields depth-first sequence, not breadth-first sequence.

questions.prompt: How does Swift Collections Deque improve queue operations over standard Swift Array in BFS?

options.text: It runs operations concurrently using Grand Central Dispatch queues.
options.explanation: Deque is a data structure, not an asynchronous dispatch queue.

options.text: It provides amortized O(1) removals from the front using a ring buffer.
options.explanation: Deque avoids shifting elements by managing head and tail offsets across a ring buffer.

options.text: It compresses node pointer references using weak tables.
options.explanation: Deque does not compress pointers or manipulate reference tables.

options.text: It sorts all inserted elements automatically on insertion.
options.explanation: Deque preserves insertion order without sorting.

questions.prompt: Which traversal order would you pick to serialize a tree so that it can be reconstructed easily?

options.text: In-order traversal storing leaf pointers.
options.explanation: In-order traversal alone cannot determine the root node without another traversal.

options.text: Post-order traversal without null child markers.
options.explanation: Post-order without null markers cannot uniquely reconstruct a general binary tree.

options.text: Pre-order traversal with null markers for empty children.
options.explanation: Pre-order visits the root first, allowing immediate node construction followed by left and right subtrees.

options.text: Reverse in-order traversal using heap sort queues.
options.explanation: Reverse in-order is not a standard serialization format.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare breadth-first search and depth-first search. Name the core data structure each uses and provide an example of when you would pick one over the other in an interview.

rubric.criterion: Identifies BFS using a queue (FIFO) and DFS using a stack (LIFO or recursion)
Explains difference in traversal geometry (level-by-level vs branch-first)
Provides a clear scenario when to pick one (e.g. shortest path for BFS, subtree/path search for DFS)

questions.modelAnswer: Breadth-first search explores a tree level by level using a first-in, first-out queue. Depth-first search dives deep along one branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. In an interview, I choose BFS when finding the shortest path in an unweighted tree. I choose DFS when checking for path existence or performing bottom-up subtree calculations.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain pre-order, in-order, and post-order depth-first search traversals. Mention the order in which root, left child, and right child are visited, and describe a key use case for in-order traversal.

rubric.criterion: Defines pre-order (root, left, right), in-order (left, root, right), and post-order (left, right, root)
Explains that in-order traversal of a binary search tree produces sorted order
Uses clear technical terminology without unnecessary jargon

questions.modelAnswer: Pre-order visits the root first, then the left and right subtrees. In-order visits the left child, then the root, and finally the right child. Post-order visits both children before visiting the parent. On a valid binary search tree, an in-order traversal visits all values in strictly sorted ascending order.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how to isolate individual tiers during a breadth-first search. Explain how capturing queue count prevents child nodes from mixing into the current level.

rubric.criterion: Explains taking a snapshot of queue.count before running the level loop
Explains that newly enqueued child nodes belong to the next tier and are not processed in the current loop
Explains grouping level values into a list or computing level metrics

questions.modelAnswer: To isolate individual levels in BFS, I snapshot `let count = queue.count` at the start of each while iteration. An inner loop runs exactly `count` times, dequeuing nodes from the current tier and collecting their values. Any children discovered during this step are appended to the queue, but they will only be processed during the subsequent tier loop.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare the auxiliary space complexity of recursive depth-first search on a balanced binary tree versus a skewed binary tree. Explain what happens to the system call stack in each case.

rubric.criterion: States O(log N) auxiliary space for balanced tree
States O(N) auxiliary space for skewed tree
Explains that call stack frames correspond to the height of the tree

questions.modelAnswer: Recursive depth-first search consumes stack memory proportional to tree height H. On a balanced tree with N nodes, the height is log N, requiring O(log N) call stack frames. On a completely skewed tree, each node has only one child, forming a linear list of depth N. In that worst case, the call stack grows to O(N) frames and risks a stack overflow crash.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why using Array.removeFirst() in a Swift BFS implementation is an interview trap. Describe two ways to avoid this performance issue.

rubric.criterion: Explains that removeFirst on Array shifts all remaining elements in O(K) time, causing O(N^2) total time
Proposes using an index pointer to avoid array shifts
Proposes using a Deque data structure (e.g. swift-collections)

questions.modelAnswer: Calling `removeFirst()` on a Swift Array takes linear time because all remaining elements shift left in memory. Repeating this for N nodes degrades overall BFS runtime to O(N squared). You can avoid this trap by maintaining a read index pointer into the array without shifting elements. Alternatively, you can use a ring-buffer double-ended queue, such as `Deque` from the official swift-collections package.
